title: Psalm 140: Rescue from Men of Violence
summary: David asks the LORD to rescue him from evil and violent men who plan harm, stir up conflict, and speak with tongues as poisonous as snakes. He describes their hidden traps, confesses the LORD as his God and the strength of his salvation, and asks that their own schemes fall back on them. The psalm ends in confidence that the LORD upholds justice for the poor and that the upright will dwell in his presence.
story: Psalm 140 opens a group of four prayers of David for rescue (Psalms 140 to 143) that follow the reflective Psalm 139. That psalm ended by asking God to slay the wicked and to search the psalmist's own heart; Psalm 140 names the wicked more concretely, describing their plans, words, and traps. The four prayers share vocabulary (snares, nets, traps, the wicked, the righteous) and together form a sustained cry of a man under attack. They lead to Psalm 144, a royal psalm of victory, and Psalm 145, the great hymn to God's kingdom, so that the Psalter's final Davidic collection moves from danger to praise.
historical:
The heading reads “For the choirmaster. A Psalm of David.” As with other superscriptions, the attribution to David is traditional, and scholars debate how to read it: as a statement of authorship, a record of a Davidic collection, or a later heading added as the Psalter was compiled. The psalm names no occasion. Readers who connect it with David's life have pointed to his years as a fugitive from Saul, when enemies spread lies about him at court (1 Samuel 24:9 and 26:19), or to Absalom's revolt, but the psalm itself gives no historical clues. Its language of slander and plotting describes the kind of opposition faced by many people in positions of responsibility, and it was preserved for use in public worship.

The word Selah appears three times (verses 3, 5, and 8). Its meaning is uncertain. It may mark a musical pause, an instrumental interlude, or a point where the singers raised their voices, but no one knows for certain.
cultural:
The images in the psalm come from hunting and warfare. Verse 5 describes a snare, the cords of a net spread along a path, and lures, the equipment used to catch birds and small animals. Hunters in the ancient Near East laid spring-traps and nets along paths where animals passed; the victim walked into them unaware. The psalmist feels hunted in the same way, by enemies who hide their intentions. Verse 7 pictures God shielding his head in the day of battle, the helmet of an ancient soldier.

The tongue as a serpent and venom on the lips (verse 3) reflects a culture that took words seriously as weapons. In a society where honor, legal standing, and livelihood depended on reputation, slander could destroy a person as surely as a sword. The imagery of burning coals and pits in verse 10 recalls God's judgment on Sodom and Gomorrah (Genesis 19:24) and Korah's rebellion (Numbers 16:31-33), when the earth opened and swallowed the rebels.
literary: Psalm 140 is an individual lament with a clear shape. Verses 1 to 5 are the complaint and plea, in two parallel stanzas each beginning with a request (rescue me, guard me) and each describing the enemies' violence, words, and traps. Verses 6 to 8 are a confession of trust and a plea that God not grant the wicked their desires. Verses 9 to 11 are imprecations, requests that the enemies' own evil return on them. Verses 12 and 13 close with a statement of confidence. The imprecations are built on a principle found often in the Psalms: the trouble the wicked cause should fall back on their own heads. Their lips caused mischief (verse 9), so let it cover them.

outline.t: Rescue me from men who plan evil and speak venom
Guard me from their hidden traps
You are my God, my strength and shield
Let their evil return on them
The LORD upholds justice for the poor

doctrines.note: The psalm trusts that God will turn the schemes of the violent back on them. Justice in the Psalms often takes this form: evil proves self-destroying, and God ensures that it does.

The LORD is called the strength of my salvation, the one who shields the psalmist's head in battle. Salvation here is concrete deliverance from danger, grounded in a personal relationship: You are my God.
The psalm describes sin not only as violent acts but as scheming hearts and poisonous words. Evil begins in plans devised in the heart and spreads through speech before it becomes violence.

words.note: Chamas, violence. The word describes wrongdoing that destroys life and social order, and it is the word used for the violence that filled the earth before the flood (Genesis 6:11). In this psalm it appears three times to describe the psalmist's enemies. It includes physical harm but also injustice, fraud, and the abuse of power.

Selah. The meaning of this word, which appears more than seventy times in the Psalms, is uncertain. It may indicate a musical pause, a change in accompaniment, or a place for emphasis. In Psalm 140 it falls after each description of the enemies' threat, as though marking a moment to pause and weigh it.

Ani, poor or afflicted. The word describes people who are economically poor and socially vulnerable, often oppressed by the powerful. The psalm ends by declaring that the LORD upholds justice for them. The psalmist places himself among the afflicted whom God defends, not among the powerful who scheme.

christ: Paul quotes the language of verse 3 in Romans 3:13, as part of a chain of Old Testament texts showing that all people, Jew and Gentile alike, are under the power of sin. The poison of vipers on human lips becomes, in Paul's hands, a description of the human condition apart from God's grace. That shift is important: the psalm's enemies are not merely a separate category of evil people, but a picture of what every human heart can become. The psalm's confidence that the LORD upholds justice for the poor and defends the needy points toward Jesus, who announced good news to the poor (Luke 4:18) and who himself was surrounded by those who laid traps for him with their words (Luke 11:53-54). Jesus did not call down fire on his enemies, and he rebuked his disciples when they wanted to (Luke 9:54-55); instead he entrusted himself to the one who judges justly (1 Peter 2:23).

hard.q: Is it right to pray that burning coals fall on our enemies?
hard.a: Verses 9 to 11 ask that the enemies be covered with their own trouble, that burning coals fall on them, and that they be thrown into fire and pits. Like other imprecatory psalms, this prayer can seem at odds with Jesus' command to love enemies. Several things should be kept in view. The psalmist is asking God to act, not planning to act himself; he hands his case to the divine judge. The requests follow the principle that evil should rebound on those who plan it, which is a request for justice rather than personal revenge. And the enemies are men of violence who threaten the poor and needy (verse 12), so the prayer is also a plea for the vulnerable. Christians read such prayers in different ways. Some see them as legitimate cries for justice that believers may still pray, especially against systemic evil, while leaving the outcome to God. Others see them as expressions of the old covenant that Jesus' teaching transforms, so that Christians pray for the repentance of their enemies. Both readings agree that vengeance belongs to God (Romans 12:19), and that the prayer is to be handed to him rather than carried out.

questions: The psalmist describes words as venom. When have words done you real harm, and when have your words harmed someone else?
The psalm ends by trusting that the LORD upholds justice for the poor. How does that confidence change the way a person responds when they are wronged?
What difference does it make to hand your case against someone over to God instead of pursuing it yourself?
